hero.label: Drug biography · No. 001
hero.line: From a gene nobody wanted to chase, to the first antibody aimed at a cancer-causing protein, told in dated, sourced chapters.
hero.spec: HER2-targeted monoclonal antibody · first FDA approval Sept 25, 1998 · brands: Herceptin, Herceptin Hylecta

chapters.title: A gene called HER2
chapters.line: A Genentech scientist cloned a growth gene called HER2, and a colleague made a mouse antibody that blocked it.
body: In 1985, Axel Ullrich, a scientist at Genentech, cloned a human gene his team named HER2. It was closely related to neu, a cancer-causing gene in rats, and it played a part in how cells grow and divide.

Also at Genentech, H. Michael Shepard's lab made a mouse antibody called 4D5 that latched onto HER2 and slowed the growth of cancer cells carrying too much of it. Once humanized, 4D5 became trastuzumab, the first antibody aimed at a cancer-causing protein.
stat: the mouse antibody that became trastuzumab

chapters.title: The aggressive kind
chapters.line: At UCLA, Dennis Slamon found HER2 overproduced in an aggressive kind of breast cancer.
body: Dennis Slamon, a physician-scientist at UCLA, heard Ullrich talk about his growth genes and asked to collaborate. Together they checked those genes against Slamon's collection of human breast tumors.

In some tumors HER2 was amplified and overproduced, and those cancers were the aggressive kind: shorter survival, more recurrence. Slamon's 1987 paper in Science made the link, and gave doctors a way to name a subtype of breast cancer: HER2-positive.
stat: of breast cancer patients have HER2-positive tumors

chapters.title: Almost abandoned
chapters.line: Genentech had doubts. A few people kept the program alive anyway.
body: Genentech was not eager. Its recent cancer projects had failed, and many inside the company doubted that an antibody could work against a solid tumor. The market also looked small, since only about a fifth to a quarter of breast cancer patients were HER2-positive.
A few people kept the program alive anyway, led by Shepard with support from Genentech vice president Bill Young.

chapters.title: An unlikely patron
chapters.line: Revlon funded Slamon's research, and the first patients were treated at UCLA.
body: Help came from outside medicine. In 1990, Revlon and its chairman Ronald O. Perelman began funding Slamon's HER2 research through a series of grants meant to speed the drug's development.
That same year, Slamon led the first clinical trial of trastuzumab in people, at UCLA.

chapters.title: Patients at the table
chapters.line: Patient advocates helped shape the trials, and a lottery shared out scarce early doses.
body: Breast cancer advocates worked with Genentech to shape the phase 3 trials, so the design reflected what patients with metastatic disease needed, and simpler entry rules sped up enrollment.

In 1995 Genentech and advocates, including Bob Erwin, whose wife had died of breast cancer, designed one of the first FDA-approved expanded access programs for a cancer drug. It opened in 1996, and because supply was short, a lottery decided who got the drug.

chapters.title: Approved
chapters.line: The FDA approved Herceptin for metastatic HER2-positive breast cancer. It added months of life, with a real cost to the heart.
body: On September 25, 1998 the FDA approved Herceptin for HER2-positive metastatic breast cancer. In the pivotal trial, 469 women were randomized to chemotherapy alone or chemotherapy plus trastuzumab. Adding trastuzumab raised median survival from 20.3 to 25.1 months, and tumors shrank in 50% of patients instead of 32%.

There was a cost. Heart damage appeared in 27% of patients who got trastuzumab with anthracycline chemotherapy, and up to 16% developed severe heart failure. With paclitaxel instead, the rate was 13%.

chapters.title: A second life
chapters.line: Approved for early-stage disease. In the HERA trial it lowered the risk of death by 26%.
body: The bigger question was whether trastuzumab could also help people with early-stage disease, after surgery. Based on two US trials, NSABP B-31 and NCCTG N9831, the FDA approved it on November 16, 2006 for node-positive early-stage HER2-positive breast cancer, alongside chemotherapy.

The HERA trial enrolled 5,102 women. After 11 years of follow-up, one year of trastuzumab after chemotherapy lowered the risk of the cancer returning by 24% and the risk of death by 26%. One year of trastuzumab became the standard of care.
stat: lower risk of death with one year of trastuzumab (HERA, 11 years)

chapters.title: Copies arrive
chapters.line: The first biosimilar copy of trastuzumab was approved.
body: On December 1, 2017 the FDA approved Ogivri (trastuzumab-dkst), made by Biocon and Mylan, the first biosimilar of trastuzumab.
It was only the second cancer biosimilar the FDA had ever approved, and the first for breast and stomach cancer.

chapters.title: Under the skin, and a prize
chapters.line: A version given under the skin was approved, and its three pioneers shared the Lasker Award.
body: On February 28, 2019 the FDA approved Herceptin Hylecta, trastuzumab combined with hyaluronidase so it can be given as an injection under the skin instead of through a vein.
That September, Ullrich, Shepard and Slamon shared the Lasker-DeBakey Clinical Medical Research Award for discovering and developing Herceptin.

chapters.title: A family of HER2 drugs
chapters.line: Trastuzumab is now the backbone of a family of HER2 drugs, including Kadcyla and Enhertu.
body: Trastuzumab became the foundation for a family of HER2 drugs. Genentech's pertuzumab, launched in 2012, is given together with it.
Two antibody-drug conjugates use trastuzumab to deliver chemotherapy straight to HER2-positive cells: trastuzumab emtansine (Kadcyla) and trastuzumab deruxtecan (Enhertu).
